Author: @jmc1151
Content:
People who call veganism a "psyop" usually come from a conspiratorial mindset, believing it's some kind of manipulation to weaken people, control populations, or push an agenda. This often stems from distrust of corporations, governments, and media—which, to be fair, *do* have a history of deception. However, the idea that veganism itself is a psyop ignores the reality that industrial animal agriculture is one of the biggest *actual* corporate-backed systems, deeply tied to environmental destruction, government subsidies, and misleading nutritional propaganda.  

If anything, the real "psyop" has been normalizing factory farming, hiding its horrors from the public, and convincing people that eating animals is necessary for health. The dairy industry literally paid for ads claiming milk gives you strong bones while suppressing studies on plant-based calcium. So, rather than veganism being a psyop, it's often the *anti-vegan* narratives that are artificially propped up by corporate interests.  

Of course, there are valid discussions to be had about the way plant-based products are being commercialized, the role of ultra-processed vegan foods, and the ethics of how vegan messaging is presented. But dismissing veganism as a psyop feels like a way to avoid engaging with the actual ethical, environmental, and health reasons behind it.

Content:
Plant based dieter here! I completely agree that veganism is more about ethics than it is about health. I’ve an autoimmune disease that makes me prone to rheumatic pains and ever since going whole plant based I’ve stopped needing analgesics (pain relievers like tramadol or prednisone) or “anti-inflammatories?” (like ibuprofen or other meds for inflammation). Now I’m 6 months into the diet, I’ve finally been able to gain muscle, my chronic fatigue is manageable now, and many other aspects that I wasn’t anticipating to fix have given me a more quality in life. If anyone is considering in researching and maybe seeing if this diet also is for you, I recommend the book “How not to Die” by Dr. Michael Greger and “The Mind-Gut Connection” by MD Emeran Mayer. Even if you don’t end up trying the diet, they have a lot of useful information to tweak and add to your current diet that will work for your specific lifestyle and situation.

Author: @MattStretz
Content: I was a vegan for 1 year, vegetarian for 7, & now I eat meat. My opinion is very centred on this topic as I was on both extremes of the spectrum. When I was a teenager I was very much an animal rights activist & while I never physically protested, I was very judgemental of meat eaters and supported organizations like peta. Then in my 20s I had an almost “rebellious” phase where I was basically a carnivore. Since then I’ve chilled out and now I’m an omnivore. All of this to say, I don’t think veganism/vegetarianism is inherently bad. When you eat a balanced diet it’s actually very healthy & the food can be very delicious. The issue is that it’s kinda hard to have that balanced diet & it’s not for everyone. You really have to plan ahead to make sure you’re eating all the things that contain the right nutrients & surprisingly most people don’t have to worry about protein intake. I find issue with people who use veganism to virtue signal & have a superiority complex. Alot of the same can also be said about the anti-vegan movement but they don’t normally protest or harass the general public so they’re not seen with the same disdain as vegans. Do whatever makes you happy. And while there are alot of genuine ethical concerns with factory farming, the horrible conditions some of these animals go through, & the environmental impact of producing such a large volume of animals, eating meat isn’t inherently unethical. I recommend EVERYONE regardless of your stance on meat consumption to read the book, The Omnivore’s Dilemma. It’s very thought provoking & makes valid arguments for both sides of the spectrum. Just some food for thought

Author: @SBChaevok
Content:
I grew up in a family where my uncles took me hunting when I was 9 or 10, and my aunt took me to an ethical ranch one of my "uncles" owned (just a family friend), to teach me where the food comes from. I've had an understanding of that since I was young. I didn't enjoy the idea that the cute animals I just met were going to become dinner over time. That said, I gave it some serious thought from that day forward... back then, I came to the conclusion that it's the cycle of life, and I'm OK participating in it. As I've grown, I more just hate the meat industry for how deplorable they are, and the conditions they keep their livestock in, en mass. 

I make every effort I can to shop ethically, buy from local butchers and brands that don't participate in the horrendous treatment of animals. I realize that's a privilege, but a privilege I've worked hard to enjoy. I wish there was more we could do to shift the livestock industry into ethical ranching practices, but if you have the means, support ethical ranching.

Edit: Also, the people that are virtue signaling their veganism are indeed frustrating. They breed contempt for the real movements out there to create sustainable ranching projects... Also, the hypocrisy boggles my mind. They do deep dives on the meat industry, but if they looked into the source of their "vegan" food... they would be surprised how horrible these companies are for the earth, surrounding biomes and overall health of the earth. We need to be focused on sustainable farming, ranching, and food production.

Author: @ADSN70919294
Content: I’m a carnivore… for health reason, not as a virtue. I’ve struggled with my weight, stomach ulcers, insomnia and chronic pain for decades… I tried every diet imaginable.. except pills, I’ve never believed in any magic pill method.. but I exhausted everything with very minimal results and always plateaued, then I went keto, which was extremely beneficial,but still didn’t alleviate all of my chronic pain.. a lot of it, but not all… and did nothing to alleviate my stomach ulcers. About a year ago I went full carnivore… mind you, that doesn’t mean all bacon and butter… people seem to think that carnivore is an “all the bacon you can eat” diet… you have to avoid the processed meats… I eat cage free eggs and poultry (locally sourced), grass fed beef and dairy (no milk), wild caught fish.. the only pork I eat are plain pork rinds, occasionally and usually as part of a recipe.. like to coat my air fried chicken. Recently I have incorporated the occasional asparagus, avocado or salad.. maybe once or twice a month, just because I really like and miss those particular vegetables, but when I do it does sometimes upset my stomach. There are right and wrong ways to do a carnivore diet. The biggest mistake people make is too much bacon and cheese (especially shredded cheese which contains starch), and deli meats… all of which will cause health issues. The only supplements I take are for my COPD… NAC and Mullen otherwise, I’m healthier, have more energy, sleep like a baby, and feel better than I have ever felt in my life. The key, though, is whatever diet one chooses to have… it’s processed food that is the enemy. The ingredients of the packaged food you buy should just be that food and maybe a bit of salt and water… if you can’t pronounce it or don’t know what it is, maybe just don’t eat it.

Author: @angryclown1990
Content:
The ethical arguments of veganism are valid. Commercial farming is horribly unethical, mistreats livestock animals in a way that is sickening, is horrible for the environment (commercial farming is responsible for deforestation, soil depletion and errosion, and more carbon pollution than every internal combustion engine in the world combined. The only things that produce the same amount of carbon pollution are mines and power plants) and GMOs in meat and produce are making our food more unhealthy than ever. 

However, humans are omnivors. You HAVE to eat meat to be healthy. It is not a choice. Our bodies have adapted to metabolize certain materials from many different sources. We aren't herbovores. Our bodies can not process plant based protine efficiently. We get protine from meat. Our bodies can only use 20 to 30% of plant based protein compared to 60 to 70% from red meat, and up to 80% or more from fish and poultry. We also get heavy minerals like sodium and iron from meat. 

All things in moderation. You need meat, you need fruit, you need grains, you need vegetables. You need a balanced diet, you need to stay active, you need to have discipline and not over consume beyond what you burn every day. Ignore all the psudo-science BS. The same rules about nutrition and health are as true today as they were when we were cavemen. There is no inovation, we aren't discovering anything new. 

Eat what you need. Eat in balance. Enjoy snacks. Indulge within reason. Get up and move around. Be active. Go to the gym if you can, if you can't do simple workouts at home. Follow the Mediterranean diet, which is scientifically proven to be the most balanced and beneficial meal structure. Buy your food from local small farms. Or just shop at aldi's or trader joe's

Be healthy, be happy, and be kind to each other and the planet.
